decks.title: Motion in a Straight Line — Part 1: Position, velocity, calculus and acceleration
goals: Distinguish path length from displacement and average speed from average velocity
Explain instantaneous velocity as a limit and find it by differentiating x(t)
Differentiate x^n, sin x, cos x, e^x and ln x, and integrate x^n between limits
Define acceleration as dv/dt and interpret its sign together with that of velocity

slides.narration: A cyclist on a canal road, a train on its track and a ball in the air all move along a line. To describe any of them we must say where it is, measured from what, and in which direction. In this part we set up the position axis, meet velocity as a rate of change, and learn the small amount of calculus that physics needs.

slides.heading: Frame of reference and point mass
slides.body_md: Motion is always described **relative to a frame of reference**: an origin, an axis and a clock.
bullets: Along a line choose an **origin** O and a **positive direction**; the **position** x is the signed distance from O.
A body is a **point mass** when its size is negligible compared with the distances it moves, so one position describes it.
A body is at **rest** if its position does not change with time in the chosen frame, and in **motion** if it does.
Rest and motion are **relative**: the bag on a train rack is at rest for the passenger and moving for a person on the platform.

slides.narration: Pick an origin, such as a bridge, and a positive direction along the road. The position of anything is its signed distance from the origin, positive on one side and negative on the other. A body can be treated as a point mass when its size is tiny compared with the distance it travels. Whether it is at rest or in motion depends on the frame we choose.

slides.heading: Distance and displacement
slides.body_md: A cyclist leaves home O, rides to the market A and returns to the temple B.
bullets: **Distance (path length):** total length of the route actually covered; a scalar, never negative, never decreasing.
**Displacement** $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$: the signed change of position; it depends only on the end points.
Always $|\Delta x| \le$ path length; they are equal only if the body never turns back.
Displacement can be positive, negative or zero; for a round trip it is zero.

The green arrow runs straight from the start to the finish: that is the displacement. It is shorter than the distance because the cyclist turned back.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a cyclist to the market
slides.body_md: A cyclist rides 900 m east from home to a market and then 350 m back west to a temple, taking 250 s in all. Find the distance, the displacement, the average speed and the average velocity.
bullets: Displacement $= x_\text{final} - x_\text{initial} = 550 - 0 = 550$ m east.
Average speed $= \dfrac{1250}{250} = 5.0$ m s$^{-1}$.
Average velocity $= \dfrac{550}{250} = 2.2$ m s$^{-1}$ east, smaller than the average speed.

slides.heading: Average speed and average velocity
slides.body_md: Over a time interval from $t_1$ to $t_2$:
bullets: Average velocity has a sign (direction along the axis); average speed does not.
Average speed is never smaller than the magnitude of the average velocity.
After a round trip the average velocity is zero but the average speed is not.
SI unit of both: metre per second (m s⁻¹); 1 m s⁻¹ = 3.6 km h⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table comparing distance, displacement, average speed and average velocity: definition, sign and whether it can be zero for a moving body

slides.narration: Average velocity is displacement divided by the time taken, so it has a sign. Average speed is distance divided by the time taken, so it is never negative. Because the distance is at least as long as the displacement, the average speed is never smaller than the size of the average velocity. After a full round trip the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero even though the body has been moving all along.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: two legs of a train journey
slides.body_md: A train covers the first 120 km of a line at 40 km h$^{-1}$ and the next 120 km at 60 km h$^{-1}$. Find its average speed for the whole 240 km.
bullets: Time for the first leg $= \dfrac{120}{40} = 3$ h; for the second $= \dfrac{120}{60} = 2$ h.
Average speed $= \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}} = \dfrac{240}{5} = 48$ km h$^{-1}$.
This is not the mean $\tfrac{1}{2}(40 + 60) = 50$ km h$^{-1}$: the train spends more time at the lower speed.

visual.alt: Table of the two legs of a train journey: distance, speed and time for each leg and for the whole trip

slides.narration: The first leg takes three hours and the second takes two hours, so the whole trip of two hundred and forty kilometres takes five hours. The average speed is forty eight kilometres per hour. It is not the plain mean of forty and sixty, because the train spends more time going slowly.

slides.heading: Instantaneous velocity: a limit
slides.body_md: Shrink the time interval around an instant and the average velocity settles to a value:
bullets: On the x–t graph the chord between two points is the average velocity; as the second point closes in, the chord becomes the **tangent**.
Instantaneous velocity is the **slope of the tangent** at that instant; its magnitude is the instantaneous speed.
For uniform motion the average and instantaneous velocities are equal; for non-uniform motion they differ.

slides.heading: Calculus 1: differentiation as rate of change
slides.body_md: For $y = f(x)$ the **derivative** is the rate of change of $y$ with $x$:
bullets: First principles for $y = x^2$: $\dfrac{(x+\Delta x)^2 - x^2}{\Delta x} = 2x + \Delta x \to 2x$.
The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives; apply the rule term by term.
In motion: $v = dx/dt$ and $a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2$.

slides.narration: The derivative of a function is the limit of the change in the function divided by the change in the variable. Working from first principles for x squared gives two x plus a tiny bit that vanishes, so the derivative is two x. The general rule is that x to the n differentiates to n times x to the n minus one. A constant gives zero, a constant factor stays, and sums are done term by term.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: from position to velocity and acceleration
slides.body_md: A particle moves along a line with $x = 4t^3 - 3t^2 + 2t + 6$ (x in m, t in s). Find $v$ and $a$ at $t = 2$ s and the average velocity from $t = 1$ s to $t = 3$ s.
bullets: $x(1) = 9$ m and $x(3) = 93$ m, so $\bar v = \dfrac{93 - 9}{2} = 42$ m s$^{-1}$, which differs from $v(2) = 38$ m s$^{-1}$.

slides.narration: Differentiate term by term. The velocity is twelve t squared minus six t plus two, which is thirty eight metres per second at two seconds. Differentiating again gives the acceleration, twenty four t minus six, which is forty two metres per second squared at two seconds. The average velocity from one to three seconds is forty two metres per second, different from the instantaneous value because the motion is not uniform.

slides.heading: Calculus 2: derivatives of sin, cos, e^x and ln
slides.body_md: Along with $x^n$ we need four more derivatives (the angle is in radians):
bullets: The cos curve is the slope of the sin curve: it is 1 where sin crosses zero rising and 0 at the peak of sin.
$e^x$ is the one function whose slope equals its own value; $\ln x$ is its inverse, with slope $1/x$.
Negative powers are covered by the same rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{-1}\right) = -x^{-2}$.

slides.narration: The cosine curve is the slope of the sine curve. Where sine crosses zero going up, its slope is one, which is the peak of cosine. At the top of sine the slope is zero, and cosine crosses zero there. The derivative of e to the x is e to the x itself, and the derivative of the natural logarithm of x is one over x. Negative powers follow the same rule as positive ones.

slides.heading: Calculus 3: integration as the reverse
slides.body_md: **Integration** reverses differentiation. For $n \ne -1$:
bullets: The **indefinite** integral has a constant $C$ (fixed by a starting value such as $x_0$ at $t = 0$); the **definite** integral between limits has none.
The definite integral is the **area under the curve** between the limits: strips of height $v$ and width $\Delta t$ add up to it.
So $x = \int v\,dt$ and $v = \int a\,dt$; $\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v\,dt$ is the displacement.

slides.heading: Acceleration and non-uniform motion
slides.body_md: Velocity itself may change with time; the rate of change is **acceleration**:
bullets: **Uniform motion:** constant velocity, $a = 0$. **Non-uniform motion:** velocity changes; **uniform acceleration:** $a$ constant.
Same signs of $v$ and $a$: speeding up; opposite signs: slowing down (retardation).
$v = 0$ at an instant does **not** mean $a = 0$: a ball at the top of its flight has $v = 0$ and $a = -g$.
SI unit of acceleration: metre per second squared (m s⁻²).

rows: about to move or to turn round

visual.alt: Table of the signs of velocity and acceleration and whether the body is speeding up or slowing down

math: \bar a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}, \qquad a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}
slides.narration: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, the derivative of velocity with respect to time, or the second derivative of position. When velocity and acceleration have the same sign the body speeds up, and when the signs are opposite it slows down. Velocity can be zero for an instant while acceleration is not, as at the top of a throw.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a particle that turns back
slides.body_md: A particle has $x = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$ (m, s). Find when it is at rest, its acceleration then, and its displacement, distance and average speed in the first 4 s.
bullets: Displacement $= 4$ m. Distance $= 4 + 4 + 4 = 12$ m (it turns back at both instants).
Average speed $= \dfrac{12}{4} = 3$ m s$^{-1}$, but the average velocity is only $\dfrac{4}{4} = 1$ m s$^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Position-time graph of a particle that moves forward to 4 metres at one second, comes back to the origin at three seconds and goes forward again to 4 metres at four seconds
visual.caption: The tangent is horizontal at the two turning instants.

slides.narration: Setting the velocity to zero gives rest at one second and three seconds. The particle goes forward four metres, comes back four metres, then goes forward four metres again. So in four seconds its displacement is four metres but the distance is twelve metres. The average speed is three metres per second against an average velocity of one.

slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: v = dx/dt: slope of the tangent
x^n → n x^(n−1); sin → cos; cos → −sin; e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x
x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C; limits give area or displacement
a = dv/dt; sign rules decide speeding up or slowing down

visual.alt: Summary table of distance and displacement, average and instantaneous velocity, derivatives, the integral of x to the n and acceleration

slides.narration: To sum up. Distance is never less than the size of displacement. Average velocity is displacement over time, average speed is distance over time. Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position, the slope of the tangent. Learn the derivatives of x to the n, sine, cosine, e to the x and log x, and the integral of x to the n. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, and its sign relative to velocity tells us whether the body speeds up or slows down.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: State the origin and positive direction; give the direction with every displacement and velocity.
Average speed over several stages = total distance ÷ total time, never the mean of the speeds.
Differentiate term by term and show the rule used; write the units of v and a at the end.
For a definite integral write the antiderivative in square brackets with limits, then subtract. Do not forget C when no limits are given.
Common mistakes: using $v = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$; adding displacements as distances; leaving out the negative sign of a retardation.

visual.alt: Table comparing distance, displacement, average speed and average velocity: definition, sign and whether it can be zero for a moving body

slides.narration: Always say what is positive. Average speed is total distance over total time. In calculus questions show the rule you use, differentiate each term, and write units. In a definite integral, substitute both limits; in an indefinite one, add the constant. Marks are lost for treating zero velocity as zero acceleration and for adding displacements as if they were distances.

slides.narration: In this part we turn motion into pictures. Graphs of position, velocity and acceleration against time show uniform velocity and uniform acceleration at a glance. Then we derive the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion in three different ways, and finish with bodies falling or thrown upward under gravity.

slides.heading: Uniform and non-uniform motion on graphs
slides.body_md: Each kind of motion has its own shape on the three graphs:
bullets: **Uniform velocity:** s–t is a straight line (slope = $v$); v–t is horizontal; a–t lies on the axis ($a = 0$).
**Uniform acceleration:** s–t is a parabola whose slope grows; v–t is a straight line (slope = $a$); a–t is horizontal.
**Non-uniform acceleration:** v–t is a curve, a–t is not horizontal; the tangent slope still gives $a$.
A graph shows one quantity against time; it is not a picture of the path in space.

slides.heading: Reading slope and area
slides.body_md: On every motion graph, **slope** and **area** carry meaning:
bullets: Slope of the s–t graph = velocity; slope of the v–t graph = acceleration.
Signed area under the v–t graph = displacement; area above the axis counts forward, below counts backward.
Signed area under the a–t graph = change in velocity.
For distance, add the areas without signs.

slides.narration: The slope of a position time graph is the velocity, and the slope of a velocity time graph is the acceleration. The signed area under a velocity time graph is the displacement, with area below the axis counting backwards. For the distance, add all areas as positive numbers. slides.heading: Equations of uniformly accelerated motion
slides.body_md: For **constant** acceleration $a$, a body with initial velocity $u$ has, after time $t$, velocity $v$ and displacement $s$:
bullets: Three methods derive them: **graphical** (areas and slopes), **calculus** (integrate $a$) and **analytical** (definitions and algebra).
Also useful: $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ and the distance in the $n$th second, $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$.
They hold only while $a$ is constant, and along one line with signs for direction.

slides.narration: For constant acceleration there are three equations: v equals u plus a t, s equals u t plus half a t squared, and v squared equals u squared plus two a s. We derive them by the graphical method using areas and slopes, by calculus using integration, and by the analytical method using definitions and algebra. They hold only while the acceleration stays constant.

slides.heading: Graphical method: v–t graph
slides.body_md: The v–t line runs from $u$ at $t = 0$ to $v$ at time $t$ with slope $a$.
bullets: **Slope:** $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, so $v = u + at$. [first equation]
**Area** (rectangle $ut$ plus triangle $\tfrac{1}{2}(v-u)t$): $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}(v - u)t$; with $v - u = at$, $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. [second]
**Trapezium form:** $s = \dfrac{(u + v)}{2}t$.

slides.heading: Graphical method: the third equation
slides.body_md: Use the area of the trapezium, $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$, and eliminate $t$ with the slope.
bullets: The area of the trapezium is its average height $\tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)$ times its base $t$.
The slope gives $t$ in terms of $v$, $u$ and $a$; substituting removes time.
The result has no $t$: use it when time is neither given nor asked.

Multiply the two and the product of u plus v and v minus u is v squared minus u squared, so s equals v squared minus u squared over two a. Rearranged, v squared equals u squared plus two a s.

slides.heading: Calculus method
slides.body_md: Start from the definitions $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$ and $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$ with $a$ constant.
bullets: Integrating $a$ once with respect to time gives velocity; integrating velocity gives displacement.
To remove time, write $a = v\,dv/dx$ and integrate with respect to position.
Limits ($t = 0$: velocity $u$, displacement $0$) fix the constants.

math: a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{dx}\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx} \;\Rightarrow\; \int_u^v v\,dv = a\int_0^s dx \;\Rightarrow\; \tfrac{1}{2}(v^2 - u^2) = as
slides.narration: In the calculus method, integrate the constant acceleration from zero to t: the change in velocity is a t, so v equals u plus a t. Put this velocity into d x by d t and integrate again: the displacement is u t plus half a t squared. For the third equation write a as v d v by d x, integrate both sides, and the half of v squared minus u squared equals a s.

slides.heading: Analytical method
slides.body_md: No graph and no integral: use the definitions and algebra.
bullets: The definition of constant acceleration gives the first equation at once.
When velocity changes uniformly, the mean velocity is the mean of the first and last values.
Squaring the first equation and replacing $ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ by $s$ gives the third.

rows: s = u t + ½ a t²

math: \bar v = \dfrac{u + v}{2}\ \text{(velocity changes at a constant rate)} \;\Rightarrow\; s = \bar v\,t = \dfrac{(u + v)t}{2} = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2
v^2 = (u + at)^2 = u^2 + 2ut\cdot a + a^2t^2 = u^2 + 2a\left(ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2\right) = u^2 + 2as
slides.narration: The analytical method starts with the definition of acceleration, which gives v equals u plus a t. Because velocity changes at a steady rate, the mean velocity is u plus v over two, and displacement is mean velocity times time. Substituting for v gives the second equation. Squaring the first equation and collecting terms gives v squared equals u squared plus two a s.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: braking a goods train
slides.body_md: A goods train moving at $54$ km h$^{-1}$ is brought to rest by a uniform retardation over 150 m. Find the retardation and the time taken.
bullets: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{0 - 225}{2 \times 150} = -0.75$ m s$^{-2}$ (a retardation of 0.75 m s$^{-2}$).
$v = u + at \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{0 - 15}{-0.75} = 20$ s. Check: $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t = \tfrac{1}{2}(15)(20) = 150$ m.

slides.narration: The distance in the sixth second is the distance in six seconds minus the distance in five seconds. slides.heading: Motion under gravity
slides.body_md: A body moving under gravity alone has the **same** acceleration, whatever its mass:
bullets: **Free fall:** acceleration $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$ **downward**, at all times: rising, at the top and falling (air resistance neglected).
Taking **up as positive** a thrown body has $a = -g$; taking down as positive, a dropped body has $a = +g$. Choose once and keep the signs.
**Dropped from rest:** $v = gt$, $y = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$; distances in successive seconds are in the ratio $1 : 3 : 5 : \dots$.
In a vacuum a feather and a stone fall together; in air the feather is held back by air resistance.

slides.narration: Near the Earth every body, heavy or light, has the same downward acceleration, about nine point eight metres per second squared, if air resistance can be ignored. Choose a direction as positive and keep the signs. For a body dropped from rest the speed is g t and the distance is half g t squared, so the distances in successive seconds are in the ratio one, three, five and so on.

bullets: Time of ascent = time of descent; the ball returns to the hand with the same speed $u$, directed downward.
At every height the speed going up equals the speed coming down.
The v–t graph is one straight line of slope $-g$; the area above the axis (rise) equals the area below (fall), so the net displacement is zero.

slides.body_md: Up positive: $v = u - gt$ is a straight line from $+u$ down to $-u$.

slides.body_md: A stone is thrown vertically upward at 14.7 m s$^{-1}$ from the edge of a 49 m high tower. Find the greatest height above the tower and the time to reach the ground below. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$)

$(t - 5)(t + 2) = 0$, so $t = 5$ s (the root $-2$ s is rejected). Speed on landing: $v = 14.7 - 9.8(5) = -34.3$ m s$^{-1}$, i.e. 34.3 m s$^{-1}$ downward.

slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Slope of s–t = v; slope of v–t = a; signed area under v–t = displacement
v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as
a = g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward for every body without air resistance
t = u/g to the top; H = u²/2g; flight 2u/g; return speed u
One line of slope −g from +u to −u; equal areas above and below

visual.alt: Summary table of motion graphs, the equations of uniform acceleration, their three derivations, free fall and motion thrown upward

slides.narration: To sum up. On graphs, slopes give rates and signed areas give changes. For constant acceleration use v equals u plus a t, s equals u t plus half a t squared, and v squared equals u squared plus two a s, and be ready to derive them graphically, by calculus and analytically. Under gravity the acceleration is nine point eight metres per second squared downward, the time up equals the time down, and the ball returns with the speed it started with.

notes.title: Motion in a Straight Line — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Frame of reference, distance, displacement, speed and velocity
sections.body_md:
- Motion is described relative to a **frame of reference** (origin, axis, clock). A **point mass** is a body whose size can be ignored compared with the distances involved. A body is at **rest** if its position does not change with time in the chosen frame and in **motion** if it does; both are relative.
- On a line we pick an origin and a positive direction. The **position** $x$ is signed. **Displacement** $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ depends only on the end points; **distance** (path length) is the length of the route and is never negative. Always $|\Delta x| \le$ distance.
- **Average velocity** $\bar v = \Delta x/\Delta t$ (signed); **average speed** = distance $/\Delta t$. A cyclist who rides 900 m east and 350 m back west in 250 s has distance 1250 m, displacement 550 m east, average speed 5.0 m s⁻¹ and average velocity 2.2 m s⁻¹ east.
- For two equal distances at 40 and 60 km h⁻¹ the average speed is 48 km h⁻¹, not the mean 50 km h⁻¹.
- **Instantaneous velocity** $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\Delta x/\Delta t = dx/dt$, the slope of the tangent to the x–t graph. Conversion: 1 m s⁻¹ = 3.6 km h⁻¹.

key_terms.definition_md: An origin, axes and a clock with respect to which positions and times are measured.
The signed change of position, final minus initial.
The total length of the route covered; a scalar.
The limit of Δx/Δt as Δt → 0, that is dx/dt.

sections.heading: 2. Elementary calculus for physics
sections.body_md:
- **Differentiation** measures the rate of change: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0}\dfrac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x}$. Rules: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^n) = nx^{n-1}$ (also for negative $n$), the derivative of a constant is $0$, a constant factor stays, and sums are differentiated term by term.
- Standard derivatives (angle in radians): $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln x = \dfrac{1}{x}$.
- In motion $v = dx/dt$ and $a = dv/dt$. Example: $x = 4t^3 - 3t^2 + 2t + 6$ gives $v = 12t^2 - 6t + 2$ and $a = 24t - 6$; at $t = 2$ s, $v = 38$ m s⁻¹ and $a = 42$ m s⁻².
- **Integration** reverses it: $\int x^n\,dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$ ($n \ne -1$) and $\int_a^b x^n\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\right]_a^b$. The indefinite integral needs a constant fixed by a starting value; the definite integral is the area under the curve between the limits.
- Example: $v = 3t^2 + 4t$ gives the displacement $\left[t^3 + 2t^2\right]_1^3 = 42$ m between 1 s and 3 s; with $x = 5$ m at $t = 0$, $x = t^3 + 2t^2 + 5$.
- Products, quotients, chain rule and integrals beyond $x^n$ are not needed here.

sections.heading: 3. Uniform and non-uniform motion, acceleration and motion graphs
sections.body_md:
- **Uniform motion:** constant velocity, $a = 0$. **Non-uniform:** velocity changes. **Acceleration** $a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2$ (SI unit m s⁻²); instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the v–t tangent. Same signs of $v$ and $a$: speeding up; opposite: slowing down. $v = 0$ for an instant does not mean $a = 0$.
- **Graphs.** Uniform velocity: s–t straight line, v–t horizontal, a–t on the axis. Uniform acceleration: s–t parabola, v–t straight line, a–t horizontal. The slope of s–t is $v$; the slope of v–t is $a$; the signed area under v–t is the displacement; the area under a–t is the change in velocity.
- A metro train that speeds up to 16 m s⁻¹ in 20 s, cruises 30 s and brakes in 8 s covers 704 m with accelerations 0.8, 0 and -2 m s⁻².
- A particle with $x = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$ is at rest at 1 s and 3 s; in 4 s its displacement is 4 m but its distance is 12 m.

sections.heading: 4. Equations of uniformly accelerated motion
sections.body_md:
- For constant $a$: $v = u + at$, $\;s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, $\;v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ (also $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)t$; distance in the $n$th second $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$).
- **Graphical:** slope of the v–t line gives $v = u + at$; area (rectangle $ut$ + triangle $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$) gives $s$; eliminating $t$ from $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)t$ with $t = (v-u)/a$ gives $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
- **Calculus:** $\int_u^v dv = \int_0^t a\,dt$; $\int_0^s dx = \int_0^t(u + at)\,dt$; $a = v\,dv/dx$ so $\int_u^v v\,dv = a\int_0^s dx$.
- **Analytical:** $a = (v-u)/t$; mean velocity $\tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)$ for uniform change; $s = \bar v\,t$; square $v = u + at$ and use $s$.
- Example: a train at 15 m s⁻¹ stopped uniformly in 150 m has $a = -0.75$ m s⁻² and takes 20 s. A bus from rest at 1.5 m s⁻² covers 8.25 m in its 6th second.
- The equations hold only while $a$ is constant and need signs for direction.

sections.heading: 5. Motion under gravity
sections.body_md:
- Under gravity alone (air resistance ignored) every body has $a = g = 9.8$ m s⁻² **downward**: rising, at the top and falling. Choose a positive direction and keep the signs ($a = -g$ for up positive).
- **Dropped from rest:** $v = gt$, $y = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = 2gh$; distances in successive seconds are in the ratio $1:3:5:\dots$. A coconut dropped for 2.5 s falls 30.6 m and lands at 24.5 m s⁻¹.
- **Thrown up at $u$:** time to the top $u/g$, greatest height $H = u^2/2g$, time of flight $2u/g$, return speed $u$ (downward); the speed at any height is the same going up and coming down. For $u = 29.4$ m s⁻¹: 3 s, 44.1 m, 6 s.
- The **v–t graph** is one straight line of slope $-g$ from $+u$ to $-u$; the areas above and below the axis are equal.
- From a tower 49 m high a stone thrown up at 14.7 m s⁻¹ reaches the ground after 5 s, rising 11.025 m above the tower first.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Say what is positive before using signs; give directions with displacements and velocities.
- Average speed over several stages = total distance ÷ total time, not the mean of the speeds.
- Show the rule when differentiating or integrating; write the antiderivative in brackets with limits, and add C when there are no limits.
- v–t graph: slope = a, signed area = displacement; split the area where v changes sign to get the distance.
- Derivations of the three equations: say a is constant, draw the labelled graph or write each integral, and finish with the result. Learn all three methods.
- For free fall write a = ±g explicitly and say "neglecting air resistance"; convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ first.

cards.front_md: What must be chosen before positions on a straight road can be quoted?
cards.back_md: An origin and a positive direction (a frame of reference).

cards.front_md: When can a body be treated as a point mass?
cards.back_md: When its size is negligible compared with the distances over which it moves.

cards.front_md: How does displacement differ from distance?
cards.back_md: Displacement is the signed change of position (end points only); distance is the total route length, never negative.

cards.front_md: Which is never smaller: distance or the magnitude of displacement?
cards.back_md: Distance.

cards.front_md: Write average speed and average velocity.
cards.back_md: Average speed = distance ÷ time; average velocity = displacement ÷ time.

cards.front_md: Two equal distances at 40 and 60 km/h. Average speed?
cards.back_md: 48 km/h, not 50: more time is spent at 40 km/h.

cards.front_md: Define instantaneous velocity.
cards.back_md: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\Delta x/\Delta t = dx/dt$, the slope of the tangent to the x–t graph.

cards.front_md: Convert 54 km/h to m/s.
cards.back_md: 15 m/s (divide by 3.6).

cards.front_md: State the power rule of differentiation.
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^n) = nx^{n-1}$.

cards.front_md: Differentiate $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
cards.back_md: $\cos x$ and $-\sin x$.

cards.front_md: Differentiate $e^x$ and $\ln x$.
cards.back_md: $e^x$ and $1/x$.

cards.front_md: Derivative of a constant?
cards.back_md: Zero.

cards.front_md: If $x = 4t^3 - 3t^2$, what are $v$ and $a$?
Integrate $x^n$ ($n \ne -1$).
Why does a definite integral have no constant C?
cards.back_md: The constant cancels when the lower limit value is subtracted from the upper.

cards.front_md: What does $\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v\,dt$ give?
cards.back_md: The displacement between $t_1$ and $t_2$ (area under the v–t graph).

cards.front_md: Define acceleration.
cards.back_md: Rate of change of velocity, $a = dv/dt$ (slope of the v–t graph); SI unit m s⁻².

cards.front_md: When does a body slow down in straight-line motion?
cards.back_md: When velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.

cards.front_md: A ball at the top of its flight: v and a?
cards.back_md: v = 0 but a = g downward.

cards.front_md: Shape of the s–t graph for uniform acceleration?
cards.back_md: A parabola: the slope (velocity) keeps growing.

cards.front_md: What does the area under an a–t graph give?
cards.back_md: The change in velocity.

cards.front_md: A v–t graph crosses the axis. How is the distance found?
cards.back_md: Add the areas above and below the axis without signs.

cards.front_md: List the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion.
Which equation has no time in it?
How does the v–t graph give $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$?
cards.back_md: Area = rectangle $ut$ + triangle $\tfrac{1}{2}(v-u)t$ with $v - u = at$.

cards.front_md: In the calculus derivation, which substitution removes time?
cards.back_md: $a = v\,dv/dx$, then integrate with respect to position.

cards.front_md: The equations of motion fail when what happens?
cards.back_md: When the acceleration is not constant.

cards.front_md: Value and direction of g near the Earth?
cards.back_md: 9.8 m s⁻², vertically downward.

cards.front_md: A ball is thrown up at u. Height, time to the top and time of flight?
What is the speed on return to the throwing point?
cards.back_md: The same as the speed of throw, u, directed downward.

questions.stem_md: A tiffin box rests on the seat beside a student in a bus moving steadily along a highway. A boy on the roadside says the box is moving; the student says it is at rest. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Both are right, because rest and motion are decided relative to the chosen frame of reference
Only the boy is right, because the road is fixed to the earth and rest is absolute
Only the student is right, because the box never changes its place on the seat
Neither is right, because a body that is not pushed cannot be moving

questions.solution_md: In the frame of the bus the box keeps its position, so it is at rest; in the frame of the road its position changes, so it is moving. Rest and motion are relative.

questions.stem_md: Using the v–t graph of a body moving with uniform acceleration a, derive the relation s = ut + ½at².

answer.model_answer_md: Let the velocity rise uniformly from $u$ at $t = 0$ to $v$ at time $t$. The displacement is the area under the v–t line. It is a rectangle of height $u$ and width $t$, giving $ut$, plus a triangle of base $t$ and height $v - u$, giving $\tfrac{1}{2}(v - u)t$. The slope gives $v - u = at$, so the triangle has area $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. Hence $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

questions.stem_md: Derive the equations v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² by the calculus method.

answer.model_answer_md: For a constant acceleration $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$, so $\int_u^v dv = \int_0^t a\,dt$, which gives $v - u = at$, that is $v = u + at$. Since the velocity is $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, the displacement follows from $\int_0^s dx = \int_0^t (u + at)\,dt$, and evaluating the integral gives $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. The limits come from the starting values $v = u$ and $x = 0$ at $t = 0$; the acceleration $a$ was taken outside the integral because it is constant.

marking_scheme.step: a = dv/dt integrated from 0 to t
Integrate v = dx/dt: s = ut + ½at²

questions.stem_md: Derive the equation v² = u² + 2as by the analytical method.

answer.model_answer_md: From the definition of acceleration as the change of velocity per unit time, $v = u + at$, so $t = \dfrac{v - u}{a}$. For uniform acceleration the velocity changes at a steady rate, so the mean velocity is $\dfrac{u + v}{2}$, and the displacement, which is the mean velocity multiplied by the time, is $s = \dfrac{u + v}{2}\cdot t = \dfrac{(u + v)(v - u)}{2a} = \dfrac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}$. Rearranging gives $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, which contains no time and so is used when time is neither given nor asked.

questions.solution_md: Eliminate t between v = u + at and s = ½(u + v)t.

marking_scheme.step: t = (v − u)/a from the definition of a
Mean velocity (u + v)/2 and s = ½(u + v)t

questions.stem_md: A stone dropped from a cliff covers 24.5 m in the last second before it hits the ground. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the height of the cliff.

answer.model_answer_md: Let the fall last $T$ seconds. The distance in the last second is the distance in $T$ seconds minus that in $(T-1)$ seconds: $\tfrac{1}{2}gT^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}g(T-1)^2 = g\left(T - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)$. Putting this equal to the given $24.5$ m and using $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$ gives $9.8\left(T - \tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 24.5$, so $T = 3$ s. The time of fall is therefore 3 s, and the height of the cliff is $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gT^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(3)^2 = 44.1$ m.

questions.solution_md: Difference of distances in T and T − 1 seconds.

marking_scheme.step: Last-second distance = ½gT² − ½g(T − 1)² = g(T − ½)

questions.stem_md: (a) Define distance, displacement, average speed and average velocity. [2] (b) A van goes 12 km east in 20 min, waits 10 min at a toll plaza and then goes 4 km west in 10 min. For the whole 40 min find (i) the distance, (ii) the displacement, (iii) the average speed and (iv) the magnitude of the average velocity, in km h⁻¹ where needed. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Distance is the total length of the route actually covered; displacement is the change of position, final position minus initial position. Average speed is the distance divided by the time taken and average velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken.

(b) The total time is $20 + 10 + 10 = 40$ min $= \dfrac{2}{3}$ h, and the waiting time counts in it. (i) Distance $= 12 + 4 = 16$ km. (ii) Displacement $= 12 - 4 = 8$ km east. (iii) Average speed $= \dfrac{16}{2/3} = 24$ km h$^{-1}$. (iv) Average velocity $= \dfrac{8}{2/3} = 12$ km h$^{-1}$ east, half the average speed because the van turned back.

Total time 2/3 h; average speed = 24 km h⁻¹

questions.stem_md: (a) State the power rule of differentiation and the derivatives of sin t, cos t, e^t and ln t. [2] (b) The position of a particle is x = 3 sin t + 2t² (x in m, t in s, the angle in radian). Find (i) its velocity at t = 0 and (ii) its acceleration at t = π/2 s. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The derivative of $t^n$ is $nt^{n-1}$ for any power $n$. The derivative of $\sin t$ is $\cos t$ and the derivative of $\cos t$ is $-\sin t$. The function $e^t$ is its own derivative, and the derivative of $\ln t$ is $\dfrac{1}{t}$ for positive $t$.

(b) The velocity is the first derivative of the position, taken term by term: $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3\cos t + 4t$. At $t = 0$, $v = 3(1) + 0 = 3$ m s$^{-1}$. The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity: $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -3\sin t + 4$. At $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $a = -3(1) + 4 = 1$ m s$^{-2}$.

questions.solution_md: Differentiate twice, term by term, and substitute.

marking_scheme.step: Derivatives of sin t, cos t, eᵗ and ln t stated
a = −3 sin t + 4 = 1 m s⁻² at t = π/2

questions.stem_md: The velocity of a particle on a straight line is v = 3t² − 6t (SI units). (a) Find its acceleration at t = 2 s. (c) The velocity is $3t(t - 2)$, negative from $0$ to $2$ s and positive afterwards. The displacement in the first 2 s is $8 - 12 = -4$ m, that is 4 m backward, and in the next 2 s it is $20$ m forward. Distance $= 4 + 20 = 24$ m. It exceeds the displacement because the particle turns back at $t = 2$ s and the backward part is subtracted from the displacement but added to the distance.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For constant $a$, $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$ gives $\int_u^v dv = \int_0^t a\,dt$, so $v = u + at$. With $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, $\int_0^s dx = \int_0^t (u + at)\,dt$ gives $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. To remove time, write $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$, so $\int_u^v v\,dv = a\int_0^s dx$, which gives $\tfrac{1}{2}(v^2 - u^2) = as$, that is $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

(b) Using the first equation, $v = 12 + 0.8(10) = 20$ m s$^{-1}$. Using the second equation, $s = 12(10) + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.8)(100) = 120 + 40 = 160$ m. As a check, the third equation gives $s = \dfrac{v^2 - u^2}{2a} = \dfrac{400 - 144}{1.6} = 160$ m, the same value, so the working is consistent. In every step the acceleration is taken as constant, which is true for this car while the throttle is held steady.
